We study the partitions that come from symmetry, the orbit partitions of groups acting on strings, and the structure function $h^G_x$ they induce. A set is a cell of such a partition exactly when its setwise stabiliser acts transitively on it, so $h^G_x$ is Kolmogorov's structure function restricted to $G$-homogeneous sets. For the full symmetric group this recovers all models and exactly the strong ones. For $GL(n,2)$ the cells are the linearly homogeneous sets, $h^{GL}_x$ lies in a band between $C(x)-α$ and $n-α$ with both edges attained, and some stochastic normal strings have simple structure that is invisible to linear symmetry. Writing each permutation group as a Burnside-ring type with a placement, we show that any space of symmetry hypotheses small enough to search is small enough to miss simple structure. Finally we cast the search for orbit models as value estimation on subgroup lattices, with computable bounds, certified training targets and a lattice version of Monte Carlo tree search.

title: Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast
ss_tldr: Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy.
abstract: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. Overall, we provide a controlled study of how different example-selection signals affect the interpretability of MoE reward models.

title: Disagreement-Guided Agentic Data Curation for Multimodal Safety
ss_tldr: These findings support traceable, disagreement-guided curation for multimodal safety evaluation and example selection and support traceable, disagreement-guided curation for multimodal safety evaluation and example selection.
abstract: Written safety policies in multimodal settings define categories whose visual boundaries span many contexts. We study disagreement as a signal for identifying useful synthetic boundary cases. Our pipeline generates policy-conditioned images, selects cases with target--rater or inter-rater disagreement, conditionally escalates unresolved cases, and retrieves the resulting rater-labeled examples as in-context demonstrations. On a failure-enriched multimodal safety benchmark, policy grounding reduces false negative rate (FNR) from 0.875 to 0.413 and raises F1 from 0.220 to 0.731; retrieval from 50 disagreement-selected examples further reduces FNR to 0.245, compared with 0.297 from a 350-example Regular pool. The selected memory also improves a different target-model family, with a smaller gain on a proprietary benchmark with a refined policy. In a blinded human study, experts disagree on 24% of disagreement-guided images and 17% of baseline-curated images. These findings support traceable, disagreement-guided curation for multimodal safety evaluation and example selection.

title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
ss_tldr: This work presents the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention, and identifies failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers.
abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

title: Arbor: How Search Policy Shapes Agent Behavior in System Optimization
ss_tldr: An evaluation framework for autonomous loop-based agents spanning efficiency, grounding, robustness, and depth, designed to characterize agent search behavior across long-running optimization campaigns are introduced.
abstract: Achieving peak performance on modern accelerators requires coordinated optimization across kernels, operator fusion, KV-cache management, quantization, scheduling, and communication overlap, a process that demands weeks of expert effort per model and hardware platform. We present Arbor, a system that gives autonomous agents an explicit optimization tree to reason over, backtrack through, and deepen with experience, with pluggable search policies, scored bandit traversal, parallel agent swarms, and depth-first sweep, sharing a common harness of containerized isolation, automatic rollback, and end-to-end validation. Arbor generalizes across domains: +40% to +193% on six production inference models across two GPU generations, +42.8% on LLM training, and +41% on recommendation training, where agents autonomously wrote kernel-level and framework-level optimizations spanning thousands of lines of code. In controlled ablations where every search policy receives the same agent, tree, and tools, we find that search structure shapes both the magnitude and the nature of the optimizations. The bandit achieves +30.1% through targeted framework fixes, the sweep +26.4% through deep kernel rewrites, and the swarm +33.4% by compounding independent changes. An agent-driven loop that receives the same harness, tools, and information, but selects its own targets reaches +14%, writing 4x more code per percentage point of improvement than Arbor's structured search policies. We additionally introduce an evaluation framework for autonomous loop-based agents spanning efficiency, grounding, robustness, and depth, designed to characterize agent search behavior across long-running optimization campaigns.

title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
ss_tldr: This work runs seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged, finding no harness leads consistently across models.
abstract: A coding agent is a language model inside a harness: the system prompt, the tools, and the context management that let a chat model work in a repository. Most of the engineering on these agents goes into the harness, and vendors and leaderboards credit it with score gains. Earlier studies have fixed the model and swapped the harness, but have not measured whether the swap changes the pass rate more than running the same harness again. We run seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged. No harness leads consistently across models. Where the data can bound the difference between two harnesses, the bound is 2 to 5 points, and a harness swap changes about as many task outcomes as a rerun. The exceptions are harness effects in particular pairings of model and harness, whose direction changes with the model: OpenCode trails by 8 to 9 points on one model and leads by 14 on another. Cost differences between harnesses also depend on the model, from under 10% to 3 to 4 times. Which harness is better therefore has no answer apart from the model, and a harness difference should be reported next to a rerun.

title: JUDOR: CTDE-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Co-Optimization of Joint UAV Motion and Decentralized Opportunistic Routing in Delay-Tolerant Network
ss_tldr: JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing, is presented.
abstract: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
ss_tldr: This work proposes integrating Large Language Models with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge.
abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.

title: When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
ss_tldr: Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average; the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average.
abstract: Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. A 2-opt local search, however, removes most of the gap at negligible cost, after which reallocation adds a few hundredths of a percent of tour length.

title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
ss_tldr: SuperScout is presented, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery.
abstract: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.

title: Surrogate Substitution Preserves PHI Detectability: A Multi-Detector Equivalence Study
ss_tldr: A paired protocol is proposed that scores the same spans before and after replacement with an identical panel of 11 detectors from three families, measures the substitution effect only on replaced spans, and bounds the effect with document-level cluster-bootstrap equivalence testing and posterior probabilities instead of significance tests.
abstract: Structure-preserving de-identification replaces protected health information (PHI) with realistic same-type surrogates ("Anna S." becomes "Maria S.", not [NAME]). De-identified notes are what allow clinical text to be shared for model development, and many pipelines run a second PHI detector over them as a safety net. We ask a narrow, testable question: on the spans a de-identifier actually replaces, can downstream PHI detectors still find the surrogate as well as they found the original value? We call this detectability preservation and treat it as a proxy, not as general utility. We propose a paired protocol that (i) scores the same spans before and after replacement with an identical panel of 11 detectors from three families, (ii) measures the substitution effect only on replaced spans, keeping it separate from coverage, and (iii) bounds the effect with document-level cluster-bootstrap equivalence testing and posterior probabilities instead of significance tests. Applied to a commercial transform on seven benchmarks in seven languages (1,750 documents), pooled recall on replaced spans moves from 75.9% to 74.7% ($Δ=-1.24$ points, 90% CI $[-1.65,-0.84]$), within a $\pm2$-point margin under overlap matching. The effect is not uniform: it exceeds $\pm2$ points for several detectors, for two identifier-dense non-English benchmarks, and under exact-boundary matching. Two-rater annotation of surrogates ($κ=0.79$), a same-slot counterfactual, and detector test-retest show that the residual has both generator-side and detector-side causes. On ICD-10 diagnosis classification of the same clinical documents, accuracy changes by at most 1 point under substitution, Faker surrogates, or redaction.

title: CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning
ss_tldr: CoNav-UAV is proposed, which models the target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing.
abstract: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.

title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
ss_tldr: An empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety and developing SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, which is evaluated four representative coding agents, and further evaluates whitelist-based execution control and LLM review.
abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services
ss_tldr: A procedure is presented that decides on calibration data from the workload that certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate.
abstract: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the new task restored risk control.

title: RiskWorld: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
ss_tldr: RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement, is introduced and within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.
abstract: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
ss_tldr: A deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables is proposed, supporting pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction.
abstract: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

title: Meta$^n$: Recursive Self-Improvement through Emergent Depth
ss_tldr: Meta, which keeps the meta-operation fixed and recurses on its input instead, outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families and outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families.
abstract: Self-improving LLM agents refine answers, not the process that produces those answers. Systems that add a meta-level hold that level fixed, and those that edit themselves must leave part of their own editing machinery untouched to stay stable, capping the meta-depth they realize at roughly two. We present Meta$^n$, which keeps the meta-operation fixed and recurses on its input instead. That operation, $Ω$, is applied repeatedly to its own products, reading the traces of the solver stack below together with the code that produced them, then writing the next layer as a strategic pre-process and a library of callable helpers. Because $Ω$ never changes, it cannot destabilize the system, and because its input strictly grows, each layer reasons from a higher vantage than the last. Depth is set by convergence rather than fixed in advance, and an evolutionary archive searches over layer chains. Across two backbones, Meta$^n$ outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families. The sharpest case is ARC-AGI-2, built to resist skill memorization, where it alone scores above zero. Ablations indicate that most of the gain from recursion comes from the conditioning each layer passes to the next, and distinct layer roles emerge with depth although no prompt prescribes them. Code available at https://github.com/minnesotanlp/meta-n

title: A Geometric Coding Theorem
ss_tldr: This result is a coding-theoretic restatement of a theorem of Trejo, Kreinovich and Longpr\'e, who showed that the complexity of describing a string by a symmetry with that string as its unique fixed point equals its Kolmogorov complexity.
abstract: This paper establishes a direct analogue of the classical Coding Theorem in the setting of symmetry groups. We consider computable bijections on the set of binary strings and define the symmetry prior of a string x as the probability that a randomly chosen symmetry from a given group G has x as its unique fixed point. We show that for any fix-retractable symmetry group G, a group admitting a computable section that selects an isolating symmetry for every string, the symmetry prior is a universal lower semi-computable semi-measure. In this case, the Geometric Coding Theorem holds. This result is a coding-theoretic restatement of a theorem of Trejo, Kreinovich and Longpré, who showed that the complexity of describing a string by a symmetry with that string as its unique fixed point equals its Kolmogorov complexity. Our contribution is to recast it in terms of algorithmic probability and to treat the symmetry group as a parameter, identifying fix-retractability as exactly the condition under which symmetry complexity collapses onto Kolmogorov complexity.

title: Bringing Back Rule Induction to Fluid Intelligence Research? An Initial Validation of the ARC-AGI Benchmark in Humans
abstract: Two competing perspectives on fluid intelligence (gf) measures propose that performance is primarily constrained either by working memory capacity or by the ability to induce novel relations. The first perspective is currently dominant in measurement, as evident from the use of a limited set of recurring rules, whereas the second perspective is reflected in many definitions but rarely present in measurement. The ARC-AGI benchmark predominantly requires rule induction and was proposed as a measure of gf for both humans and artificial systems. However, its psychometric properties have not yet been examined in human samples. We therefore investigated the psychometric characteristics and nomological network of ARC-AGI in a first study with 100 participants. A compilation of ARC-AGI items showed good psychometric properties and correlated substantially with figural fluid intelligence as measured by a figural reasoning test ($ρ$ = .63). Associations with figural originality were weak. These findings provide initial support for the validity of ARC-AGI as a measure of human fluid intelligence. Future research should include more rule induction tasks as well as additional multivariate covariates. This study is unusual by studying a task in humans that was initially designed for machines. We suggest systematically embedding AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities to enable more systematic evaluation and interdisciplinary cooperation.

title: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
ss_tldr: The Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE) is introduced, which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function and improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity.
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

title: Measuring What Matters: Synthetic Benchmarks for Concept Bottleneck Models
abstract: Concept bottleneck models predict using high-level concepts detected in inputs. Although these models provide a simple way to reap benefits from interpretability, they are hard to train and evaluate because very few real-world datasets include concept labels. In this paper, we develop synthetic benchmarks for concept bottleneck models. With our benchmarks, researchers can generate labeled datasets and control properties that affect performance, such as data modality, the choice of concepts, or annotation quality. They can thus find problems that suit these models and isolate the factors behind their failures. We demonstrate how our benchmarks can be used to evaluate major use cases for concept bottleneck models: decision support, i.e., helping human experts make better decisions; and automation, i.e., handling routine tasks without supervision. Our demonstrations show how the benchmarks can identify new failure modes and attribute them to either the architecture or the data.

title: LLM-Assisted Reranking to Operationalize Nuanced Objectives in Recommender Systems
ss_tldr: The results highlight the power of LLMs to operationalize contextual nuance in high-stakes political recommendation, and underscore the need to evaluate LLM-assisted personalization beyond accuracy and to treat prompt design as a value-laden choice rather than a neutral default.
abstract: Recommender systems shape what information we see, raising concerns about filter bubbles, radicalization, polarization, and social inequality. Large language models (LLMs) enable more powerful personalization that may intensify these dynamics, yet most recommenders are tuned for engagement or narrow accuracy metrics, with little attention to broader social effects. We investigate whether LLM-assisted reranking, while improving personalization, inadvertently amplifies exposure to ideologically congenial, extreme, or conspiratorial political content, a risk theorized but not yet empirically characterized. Using real YouTube trajectories, we rerank the platform's sidebar candidates by zero-shot prompting across three models, alongside an embedding baseline, and evaluate relevance, ideological alignment and diversity, and exposure to conspiratorial or extremist content. We find that (i) under a pure personalization instruction, reranking improves relevance while narrowing ideological exposure and, on two of three models, promoting problematic content for users with such histories; the third model, which declines most explicitly partisan requests, points to model-specific guardrails; (ii) lightweight prompt-level constraints substantially reduce problematic exposure on all three models, while the regularized rerankers still rank above the platform baseline on relevance; and (iii) synthetic experiments varying topical and partisan cues independently show no fixed preference between them: topic dominates on abortion and immigration, while partisanship takes over on elections, where the topical signal is weaker. Our results highlight the power of LLMs to operationalize contextual nuance in high-stakes political recommendation, and underscore the need to evaluate LLM-assisted personalization beyond accuracy and to treat prompt design as a value-laden choice rather than a neutral default.

title: Hearsay: Who Can Audit the Record a Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
ss_tldr: Hearsay is built, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task, and Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task, is built, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task.
abstract: The record of an agent's run is written by the harness that drives the agent. When the run is later disputed, the auditor was not there and has only this record. We ask whether someone who was not there can check the record, and what decides the answer. It depends on who wrote what a check can rely on: if the harness wrote all of it, the record is only the harness's own word, and we call it hearsay. We build Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, model examiners from three vendors and a human panel read the records and answer questions about the runs, and every passage they cite is labelled mechanically by who wrote it. We also audit what is deployed: in all sixteen frameworks, the harness is the only writer. With one writer, readers can name the fault from the record, in up to nine runs in ten, but they cannot check the record. The model examiners claim corroboration for 18 to 55 points more of their evidence than the labels support, a gap we then predicted for runs driven by another vendor's model and found again. And the best of them notices only half of the alterations we make to a record, while the two that name the fault most often cannot tell what a harness left out. With a second writer, the record can be checked. Our sandbox keeps a ledger of what passes between harness and model, and reading the ledger against the record in both directions shows what the record leaves out and what it adds. We test this as an auditor would use it, on one unseen record at a time. On runs driven by a third vendor's model, with every rule committed before the records existed, it reports 64 of 66 alterations and flags none of 84 clean records. On held-out records in five formats it reports 109 of 115. What makes a record evidence is a second writer, not a better reader.

title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
ss_tldr: This work introduces Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE) to test whether harness improvements survive changes to the evaluation protocol and gives conditions under which this finite archive bounds the gain loss on an ideal benchmark with shortcuts removed.
abstract: An optimized agent harness can improve on held-out tasks by relying on formatting conventions that those tasks share with the rest of the benchmark. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE) to test whether harness improvements survive changes to the evaluation protocol. A Proposer edits the harness around a fixed foundation model. A Challenger then searches for a protocol change that preserves the tasks but reduces the updated harness's gain over the initial harness. Executable checks test whether the transformation preserves task semantics. If the gain loss is confirmed on held-out tasks, CHASE adds the transformation to an archive that constrains subsequent harness updates. We give conditions under which this finite archive bounds the gain loss on an ideal benchmark with shortcuts removed. We evaluate CHASE on Syn-Ledger, OfficeQA, FinanceBench, and SWE-Bench Pro V2. On Syn-Ledger, removing the known shortcuts yields 38.30% accuracy for CHASE and 18.27% for HarnessEvolve. On the 21 certification tasks from SWE-Bench Pro V2 HARD-51, changing the issue formatting and tool-output field order reduces HarnessEvolve's gain over the initial harness from 8.57 to 3.81 percentage points. The final CHASE harness retains 10.48 points of its 11.43-point gain under the same change.

title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables
ss_tldr: This work introduces TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains under a shared cross-validation protocol, and compares classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points.
abstract: Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN 2.5 has the highest point estimate, closely followed by TabPFN 3 and Logistic Regression. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN 2.5 from TabPFN 3 by 87 Elo (95\% interval [43, 129]).   Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and reported here at the reference and full cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable. The benchmark is open to contributions of new biomedical datasets.   The interactive leaderboard is available at https://tabbench-bio.eu.

title: BearingNAS: Obtaining In-Sensor Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems for Bearings Using a Laptop
ss_tldr: BearingNAS is introduced, a HardwareAware Neural Architecture Search (HW-NAS) framework designed to shift the intelligence directly onto the sensor die via in-sensor processing, enabling low-cost, production-scale bearing fault diagnosis.
abstract: This paper introduces BearingNAS, a Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search (HW-NAS) framework designed to shift the intelligence directly onto the sensor die via in-sensor processing. BearingNAS frames the search as a constrained optimization problem targeting extreme micro-budgets (4 to 8 kiB of RAM and 16 to 32 kiB of Flash). To eliminate the reliance on expensive discrete GPUs, we propose a lightweight, derivative-free search strategy paired with a single data-flow search space that leverages a decaying kernel growth formulation to prevent parameter explosion. We evaluate our framework on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing benchmark, optimizing architectures for three STMicroelectronics targets: two commodity microcontrollers and the LSM6DSO16IS Intelligent Sensor Processing Unit (ISPU). Running entirely on a laptop CPU, the search converges in less than an hour. The resulting best in-sensor architecture achieves a highly competitive diagnostic accuracy of 99.50\% on the ISPU. These results demonstrate the viability of shifting the machine learning workload inside the sensor package, enabling low-cost, production-scale bearing fault diagnosis.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
ss_tldr: ElephantAgent is presented, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity over the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context and provides Historical Traceability, a secondary guarantee that keeps state transitions attributable and recoverable.
abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, recent tool and memory poisoning attacks can covertly bias agent behavior. We observe that such attacks mounted out of band share a single enabler: each succeeds only by presenting the agent with a contextual state (e.g., tool state and memory) that is not the latest faithfully evolved one. This observation suggests that a continuity check over the contextual state covers this family of attacks. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity over the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context. Before each planning-and-execution cycle, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest in a linearizable ledger of state transitions, maintained over replicated trusted hardware. The protocol also provides Historical Traceability, a secondary guarantee that keeps state transitions attributable and recoverable. We integrate ElephantAgent into DeepSeek Harness (DSH) and implement ElephantDSH, an agentic system protected by contextual state verification. ElephantDSH withstood all out-of-band attack attempts, from rug pulls and rollbacks to attacks on its own mechanism, and recovered from an in-band prompt injection in all trials. By comparison, existing defenses typically check only what enters the context: of the five we evaluated, all leaked the targeted content under the rollback, and three also under the rug pull. ElephantDSH completed all normal coding tasks with a relative overhead of 1.02-1.07$\times$ over the original DSH with model latency variation removed.

title: Brownian Bridge Diffusion-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Data Detection for Jamming-Resilient OFDM Receivers
ss_tldr: A Brownian bridge diffusion-assisted joint channel estimation and data detection (BBD-JCED) framework for jamming-resilient orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers is proposed and a variational lower bound is derived to reformulate the intractable bit estimate problem into a tractable training objective, providing a probabilistic foundation for the loss function design.
abstract: In next-generation wireless networks, the growing density of devices and limited spectrum resources pose severe jamming challenges to fragile legitimate communication links in the wireless electromagnetic environment. Crucially, when jamming overlaps with pilot and data symbols in both time and frequency domains, it inflicts a severe bottleneck on receiver-side joint estimation and detection. Existing schemes often lack an effective framework to combat such jamming contamination, thereby failing to guarantee reliable transmission. To address this issue, we propose a Brownian bridge diffusion-assisted joint channel estimation and data detection (BBD-JCED) framework for jamming-resilient orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers. The proposed framework consists of a jamming suppression module and a Brownian bridge-joint recovery module. The former identifies jamming-contaminated bins in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain and suppresses the dominant jamming components through spectral notching. The latter establishes a Brownian bridge-based probabilistic graph to model the probabilistic transition process from the suppressed OFDM observation to the coded bits, and performs a reverse recovery process to enable enhanced joint channel estimation and data detection. Moreover, we derive a variational lower bound (VLB) to reformulate the intractable bit estimate problem into a tractable training objective, providing a probabilistic foundation for the loss function design. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training algorithm to separately optimize the jamming suppression and Brownian bridge-joint recovery modules. Simulation results under representative jamming types demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior jamming suppression and bit recovery performance over the considered baseline schemes while maintaining competitive inference complexity.

title: SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference
ss_tldr: SharQ is introduced, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition and recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats.
abstract: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.

title: Linearized 2-Simplicial Attention
abstract: We present a linearized form of 2-simplicial attention by rewriting the trilinear score as an inner product between a composite query and a key, so that the sum over keys takes the same form as ordinary softmax attention. We then approximate this sum with positive random features and store all previous keys in a fixed-size state, while the sum over second keys stays exact over all previous tokens. This reduces the cost from cubic to quadratic in sequence length, and both keys range over all previous tokens, which windowed 2-simplicial attention does not allow. We implement it with custom Triton kernels and combine it with Kimi Delta Attention to build a model with no softmax attention at all. With 15B equal training tokens on FineWeb-Edu, this model lowers validation loss from 2.35 to 2.32 over a KDA hybrid and lowers LAMBADA perplexity from 40 to 38.

title: GA-VINO: A Geometry-Aware Variational Physics-informed Neural Operator for Mindlin-Reissner Plates
ss_tldr: This study proposes a geometry-aware variational neural operator for Mindlin-Reissner plate problems, termed MR-GVNO, which achieves millisecond-level full-field inference and favorable cross-geometry generalization.
abstract: Plate and shell structures are widely used in engineering fields. Rapid response prediction for such structures under complex geometries, heterogeneous materials, and varying loads is important for engineering design, but conventional numerical methods usually require repeated modeling and solution when the physical configuration changes. To address this issue, this study proposes a geometry-aware variational physics-informed neural operator (GA-VINO) for Mindlin-Reissner plates. GA-VINO represents the plate geometry using boundary point clouds and incorporates a material encoder, a load encoder, and a scalar-parameter branch to handle spatially random material fields, spatially varying pressure loads, and sample-level uniform parameters. Through multi-branch point cloud encoding and cross-attention, GA-VINO fuses geometric, material, loading, and query point information, and predicts the transverse deflection and rotations at arbitrary query locations. Unlike conventional data-driven neural operators, GA-VINO requires no labeled solution data during training. Instead, it minimizes a variational physics-informed loss constructed from the discretized total potential energy of the Mindlin-Reissner plate. Compared with grid-based neural operators, GA-VINO directly processes irregular point clouds and allows different physical fields to be discretized on different point sets, avoiding forced interpolation onto a common grid. The method is validated on multiple examples involving different geometries, material fields, and load distributions. The results show that GA-VINO achieves promising accuracy in deflection, rotation, gradient-sensitive, and energy-based metrics, completes full-field inference for new samples within milliseconds, and exhibits promising cross-geometry generalization capability.

title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination
ss_tldr: It is shown that innovation is implied by the condition for hallucination identified by Kalai and Vempala, and, further, that it is an almost characterization of hallucination: hallucination implies innovation, and conversely, innovation implies hallucination with high probability.
abstract: Hallucination is a central limitation of large language models (LLMs), and substantial effort has been devoted to understanding and mitigating it. Towards this, Kalai and Vempala (STOC 2024) introduced a probabilistic framework formalizing calibration and hallucination, and showed that, with high probability, calibrated LLMs hallucinate roughly at the rate of the "missing mass", a measure of how incomplete the training data is relative to its source. This raises two fundamental questions: (i) what property of a calibrated LLM makes hallucinations unavoidable? and (ii) can hallucinations be avoided by giving up calibration? We answer these questions by introducing a simpler property we call innovation that measures the tendency of a model to produce outputs outside the training data. We show that innovation is implied by the condition for hallucination identified by Kalai and Vempala, and, further, that it is an almost characterization of hallucination: hallucination implies innovation, and conversely, innovation implies hallucination with high probability. We also provide lower bounds on the hallucination rate based on the "innovation rate", and by relating innovation rate back to missing mass, we obtain new hallucination rate lower bounds based on missing mass that extend the results of Kalai and Vempala.

title: MAP: A Benchmark on Multimodal Accessibility Planning for Real World Places
ss_tldr: MAP is the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world and contains two novel assessments.
abstract: We introduce MAP, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world. In our evaluation, systems are presented with requests to verify or recommend a point of interest meeting an accessibility requirement. MAP contains two novel assessments: Claim verification for accessibility planning assesses if information on places and stated accessibility features is supported and identifies places that satisfy requested accessibility features. Visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning checks if a multimodal AI system can select visual evidence for the requested place and accessibility feature. Our methodology supports comparison of AI systems in a setting where place information and accessibility information can change over time by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times. The benchmark is based on automatic rating and human rating for a proportion of responses.

title: How do features act in an individual prediction? Separating standalone and interaction effects with a case-based taxonomy
ss_tldr: Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.
abstract: Local explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME summarize each feature with a single attribution score, and interaction indices quantify how strongly features interact. Neither tells a user how a feature acts in a given prediction: whether its effect is the same alone and in context, or whether the other features amplify it, make it unnecessary, switch it off or reverse it. We extend case-based feature importance (CBFI), originally a global method, to individual predictions. Evaluating the model in four hybrid states per background sample decomposes the in-context importance of a feature into a standalone and an interaction effect, and a case taxonomy labels each feature of an instance as inactive, standalone, amplified, redundant, gated or reversed. We compare the method with k-SII, TreeSHAP interaction values and the H-statistic on synthetic functions, and study eight real tabular datasets with six model families. On the true functions, the decomposition recovered interactions exactly (correlation 0.99 with the analytic local interaction). On fitted models, pair recovery was slightly below that of dedicated indices (local precision@k 0.86-0.91 versus 0.91-0.95). Interaction values alone could not distinguish substitution from gating, whereas the taxonomy identified both without knowing the partner (accuracy 0.74-0.76); applied to Shapley interaction values, it performed comparably. On real data, 45-57% of feature pairs with nearly identical SHAP values received different labels, and in a medical-insurance model the method showed that the interaction component of smoking changes sign at a body-mass index of 30. Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.

title: SciFigQual-Bench: Scientific Figure Quality Assessment with Manuscript-Linked Context
ss_tldr: SciFigQual-Bench is introduced, a manuscript-linked benchmark for published CS-conference figures that binds each figure to its caption and to index-resolved citing paragraphs, and scores visual clarity, layout, caption consistency, context consistency, and misleading risk, leaving a dimension unevaluated when its evidence is absent.
abstract: Scientific figure quality is bound to the manuscript: a crop can be visually clear and still contradict its caption or the paragraph that cites it. Most image quality assessment and chart-understanding methods target a detached visual surface or a question-answering score, rather than alignment among the figure, its caption, and the citing text. A single end-to-end prompt that sees the image and the text together still mixes what is visible with what the caption and the citing paragraph claim, so fluent wording can raise a visual score and missing text can be treated as low quality. To address this gap, we introduce SciFigQual-Bench, a manuscript-linked benchmark for published CS-conference figures that binds each figure to its caption and to index-resolved citing paragraphs, and scores visual clarity, layout, caption consistency, context consistency, and misleading risk, leaving a dimension unevaluated when its evidence is absent. SFQ-Agent reads the image and the text in separate calls and records modality-specific evidence. A cross-modal judge scores caption and citing-text alignment from those reports, and a deterministic runner keeps the visual scores, sets misleading risk by a fixed rule, and applies the written caps, so each dimension follows the rubric instead of a single end-to-end prompt. Experiments comparing this staged judge with single-pass and OCR-sidecar protocols find the closest point-estimate fit to mean human ratings under staged judging, while the gap between protocols remains small. Caption consistency remains the main gap, and agreement with the rater mean answers a different question from agreement among human raters. Project page: https://frankdengai.github.io/SciFigQual-Bench/

title: Robustness of Text-Only Adapted Speech LLMs for Spoken Semantic Parsing
ss_tldr: Comparisons of Speech LLMs and ASR-LLM cascades under matched text-form supervision show that Speech LLMs generally achieve better performance in command understanding, intent prediction, and function calling, while improvements in fine-grained entity prediction are less consistent.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate structured outputs from natural language instructions, including semantic frames and function calls. When the input is speech, this task becomes spoken semantic parsing, which can be performed using either Speech LLMs or ASR-LLM cascades. Although both approaches can be adapted with text-only task supervision, their relative robustness to acoustic degradation remains unclear. We compare these approaches under matched text-form supervision using 3B and 7B models across three datasets, evaluated on clean speech and babble noise at five SNR levels. Results show that Speech LLMs generally achieve better performance in command understanding, intent prediction, and function calling, particularly under severe noise, while improvements in fine-grained entity prediction are less consistent. An additional evaluation shows that Speech LLMs achieve lower average inference time per sample than ASR-LLM cascades at both model scales.

title: WorkWorlds: Evaluating Agents in a Company Built Before the Task
ss_tldr: It is argued that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder, and it is argued that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected.
abstract: Many knowledge work benchmarks are built around single tasks, where the context and files for each task are selected concurrently or after task definition. Research has argued that this construction method does not reflect real workplace work, yet the impact has never been measured under controlled conditions. To compare the two constructions under controlled conditions, we introduce WorkWorlds, an infrastructure that modularizes company components into revision, date, and employee seat to be separately adjusted. Using historical data donated by a real company, we reconstructed a pharmaceutical company, PharmaCo. Two experts with over ten years of industry experience each wrote eight tasks based on real events that occurred at the company, and each independently constructed a task-specific environment for every task. Across 192 controlled evaluations, when the agent was switched from the task-specific environment to all the materials truly visible to the employee, evidence access dropped from 90.4 percent to 72.8 percent, and the criterion pass rate dropped from 76.7 percent to 68.0 percent. However, in cases where the agent found the required evidence, the pass rates under both conditions were almost identical. Furthermore, switching between the environments built by the two experts for the same task resulted in an average pass rate difference of 6.6 percentage points. The three agents also gained by different amounts, which changed the gaps between them. We argue that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder.

title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
ss_tldr: MANGO-Grasp is proposed, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics.
abstract: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials are available at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.

title: Multi-Modal Environment-Aware Beam Management for Massive MIMO: A Geometry-Driven Virtual Base Station Framework
ss_tldr: This paper proposes a geometry-driven framework that utilizes multi-modal environmental data, specifically regional 3D light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds and location information, to construct an offline virtual base station (VBS) database and develops a hierarchical dual-agent dueling double deep Q-network for coordinated beam selection.
abstract: High-frequency massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems promise ultra-high data rates. However, efficient beam management remains challenging due to the prohibitive beam training overhead and intricate coordination required in multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) scenarios. To address these bottlenecks, environment-aware communications have emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging site-specific knowledge to circumvent exhaustive pilot-based beam training and streamline multi-user communications. In this paper, we propose a geometry-driven framework that utilizes multi-modal environmental data, specifically regional 3D light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds and location information, to construct an offline virtual base station (VBS) database. By modeling dominant reflection paths via mirror symmetry across building facades reconstructed from the point clouds, the VBS database provides a compact and sparse description of the wireless propagation environment. Given a user location, the VBS representation supports online coarse channel reconstruction and the generation of a beamspace prior. To refine the coarse estimates, we design a VBS-assisted orthogonal-pilot (VOP)-based partial beam training scheme with limited online measurements. Finally, to coordinate beam selection under inter-user interference, we develop a hierarchical dual-agent dueling double deep Q-network for coordinated beam selection (DD3QN-CBS). Simulation results show that the proposed framework improves effective spectral efficiency over the evaluated stochastic, heuristic, and conventional learning-based baselines, while achieving competitive performance with fewer online beam measurements.

title: CriticHack: Evaluating Visual Rewards Under Robot Policy Optimization
ss_tldr: Optimize shifts a policy toward outcomes that score above the executions they compete with, the executions they can take the place of, and turns low-scoring failures into both successes and wrong-object failures, even when the reward model scores successes higher.
abstract: Learned visual reward models score a robot's execution from camera images and an instruction, and are increasingly used to fine-tune robot policies. Two checks decide whether to trust one: the reward model separates successes from failures, and task success rises during training. We show that both checks can pass while the policy learns to act on the wrong object. When a diffusion policy is fine-tuned against the reward model Robometer to open a drawer, task success rises by 10.2 percentage points. Wrong-object failures, which open a different drawer, rise by 10.9 points, whereas the same training on the simulator's task-completion signal raises success alone. A second reward model, RoboReward-8B, behaves the same way, and the effect reappears on a physical robot. This happens because of how the reward scores the policy's own failures. Most failures make little progress and score low, while a wrong-object failure looks like progress and scores well above them. Optimization shifts a policy toward outcomes that score above the executions they compete with, the executions they can take the place of. It therefore turns low-scoring failures into both successes and wrong-object failures, even when the reward model scores successes higher. This rule needs only executions of the initial policy, so it can be tested before training. On a stacking task we predicted which of three object placements Robometer would exploit, and training raised wrong-object stacks from 20% to 69% in that placement and in neither of the others. The same rule gives a check to run before optimization and a repair that needs no labels: scoring each execution again on frames re-rendered with the objects the instruction does not name put back removes the amplification on both tasks and on the robot.

title: Risk-Calibrated Intent Routing for Conversational AI via Signed Lexical Evidence
ss_tldr: This work uses separate calibration data and a statistical upper bound on the error rate to set the minimum confidence required to accept a request, and develops a two-feature confidence model that improves routing by measuring how strongly the wording supports or challenges the original intent prediction.
abstract: Conversational AI has become widely used as advances in language models let people find information, get writing help, and ask for practical guidance in their own words. When an assistant handles specific tasks, it must infer what the user wants and decide whether to act on that prediction. A sentence classifier's confidence can miss clues in the wording. We combine the gap between the classifier's two highest scores with signed lexical evidence, a score based on words and short character patterns. The score is positive when those patterns favor the predicted intent and negative when they favor another. We use separate calibration data and a statistical upper bound on the error rate to set the minimum confidence required to accept a request. Across ten runs per dataset, our method reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve, which summarizes error as more requests are accepted, by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, respectively, compared with a confidence model that uses only sentence classifier scores. At a 5% error target, the share of accepted requests rises by 1.83 percentage points on BANKING77 and 5.14 points on HWU64. CLINC150 already has near-full coverage at that target. At a 2% target, calibration finds a rule that accepts some requests in all 30 runs. Our contribution is a two-feature confidence model that improves routing by measuring how strongly the wording supports or challenges the original intent prediction.

title: Cost-Efficient LLM Evaluation: A Framework for Narrow Confidence Intervals Under Fixed Budgets
ss_tldr: This work introduces a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage, and achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly important role in both academic research and industry. Reliable evaluation helps researchers understand model capabilities and assess progress during model development. However, evaluation can be costly, and researchers often need to assess performance within a fixed budget. Because model outputs can vary across runs, this budget must be allocated between testing different tasks and repeating selected tasks. A confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty in the resulting performance estimate. Obtaining narrower intervals at the same confidence level and evaluation cost provides a more precise assessment of model performance, helping researchers draw clearer conclusions from limited observations. We introduce a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage. The framework then uses disagreements between runs on the same task to bound estimation error, allowing narrower confidence intervals at the same confidence level when the sampled repeats show little variability. When repeated runs on each task yield the same outcome, we prove that our framework achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow. We establish matching lower bounds both when every task must be covered and when tasks may be skipped, even for evaluators who use earlier results to decide which run to carry out next. On LiveCodeBench, our framework yielded narrower confidence intervals on average than uniform random sampling in 15 of 16 model configurations, with a median width reduction of 30.6% at the same confidence level and the same budget of 1,100 outputs per configuration.

title: CaMBRAIN: Real-time, Continuous EEG Inference with Causal State Space Models
ss_tldr: CaMBRAIN is proposed - the first Causal, Mamba-based state space model (SSM) capable of real-time inference of EEG signals, arguing that bidirectional approaches are needlessly expensive given the causal, unidirectional nature of EEG.
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a critical, non-invasive method to monitor electrical brain activity. EEGs can span anywhere from a couple seconds to multiple hours, posing a major hurdle for existing deep learning methods due to two major factors: (1) existing EEG models are predominantly built upon the attention mechanism, incurring quadratic scaling as the sequence length increases, and (2) raw EEG signals must be processed in a sliding-window fashion due to fixed-length input requirements, preventing global understanding of the entire signal. To this extent, we propose CaMBRAIN - the first Causal, Mamba-based state space model (SSM) capable of real-time inference of EEG signals, arguing that bidirectional approaches are needlessly expensive given the causal, unidirectional nature of EEG. However, training such a model is non-trivial, as crucial EEG events can be extremely brief - within fractions of a second - yet separated by long intervals spanning minutes. Current EEG methods use self-supervised objectives that optimize for signal reconstruction, but these are not well suited for streaming SSMs; they fail to explicitly train the hidden state to retain the salient long-range context needed for streaming inference.
