Our findings emphasize the ongoing paradigm shift in the NLP landscape, i.e., the unification of downstream tasks and elimination of the need for pre-labeled training data.

title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
ss_tldr: DexWAC is introduced, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage and surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks.
abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $π_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.

title: BARE: Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion for Humanoid Robots
ss_tldr: BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability, is proposed and validated.
abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. Recent advances in reflexive evasion have focused primarily on quadrupeds, which typically rely on large-scale whole-body maneuvers. In contrast, humanoids can exploit their rich body articulation to evade through small, localized body adjustments. By moving threatened body regions without repositioning the entire body, these responses may require less execution time and less surrounding free space. However, local adjustments can alter mass distribution or support conditions, making it challenging to achieve rapid evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. To this end, we propose BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. A risk-guided motion adapter is designed to select reference motions from a retargeted human evasive motion library based on the threatened body region and to adjust their temporal phases based on collision urgency, allowing the robot to reach evasive postures before potential contact. Conditioned on the adapted reference and link-level collision risk, a reflexive evasion policy learns through reinforcement learning to coordinate local body adjustments with whole-body stabilization. We validate BARE in simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to perform targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability.

title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
ss_tldr: This work introduces ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them and evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL.
abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

title: MargEmbed-Akan: Bridging Twi Questions and English Knowledge through Cross-Lingual Score Distillation
ss_tldr: MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation, is introduced, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation that performs better on diacritic-free Twi and on Bible translation retrieval.
abstract: Most information sought online by Twi (Akan) speakers is written in English, making cross-lingual retrieval essential. We evaluate eight systems: BM25, five open embedding models, and two proprietary models (gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) on two Twi-English tasks. AfriQA contains 1,221 natively written Asante Twi questions that must retrieve their answering English Wikipedia passages. Bible translation retrieval requires a Twi passage to retrieve its English translation from 6,195 candidates.   We introduce MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation. The frozen base model scores each English training question against its answer passage and seven hard negatives. The student learns to reproduce these scores from both an NLLB-200 Twi translation that passes a round-trip translation check and the original English question, preserving English behaviour. During training, passages are encoded by the frozen base model; at evaluation, MargEmbed-Akan encodes questions and passages.   On AfriQA, base AfriE5 and gemini-embedding-001 both achieve 66.6 nDCG@10; EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large achieve 56.6, 51.3, and 53.4, respectively. MargEmbed-Akan achieves 71.5, outperforming gemini-embedding-001 by 4.9 points, its base model by 5.0, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by 18.1. Its largest gain is on Twi typed without E and O (+7.5 over gemini-embedding-001). English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, although both proprietary models score 1.5-2.2 points higher. On Bible translation retrieval, MargEmbed-Akan and gemini-embedding-001 are statistically tied on standard Twi (97.2 vs. 96.5 nDCG@10); MargEmbed-Akan performs better on diacritic-free Twi (92.7 vs. 84.9). No AfriQA data was used for training or model selection.

title: Wi-Fi Enabled Edge Intelligence Framework for Smart City Traffic Monitoring using Low-Power IoT Cameras
ss_tldr: It is shown that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models, and demonstrates the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.
abstract: Real-time traffic monitoring in smart cities demands ultra-low latency processing to support time-critical decisions such as incident detection and congestion management. While cloud-based solutions offer robust computation, their inherent latency limits their applicability for such tasks. This work proposes a localized edge AI framework that connects low-power IoT camera sensors to a client, or applies offloading of inference to an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (GPU). Networking is achieved via Wi-Fi, enabling image classification without relying on wide-area infrastructure such as 5G, or wired networks. We evaluate two processing strategies: local inference on camera nodes and GPU-accelerated offloading to the Jetson Nano.We show that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models. These results demonstrate the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.

title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
ss_tldr: This work proposes VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision and evaluates VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench.
abstract: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.

title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
ss_tldr: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it, which cannot support the conclusion that agents'hazard of failure declines as a task goes on.
abstract: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
ss_tldr: HEME, which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context, is introduced and it is shown that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.
abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

title: Branch and Consolidate: A Unified Recipe for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
ss_tldr: A unified recipe for multimodal MOPD is presented that consolidates specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint back into the single student they branched from, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists.
abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.

title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research
ss_tldr: RecurSciBench is introduced, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research and shows that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.

title: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
ss_tldr: This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments, and finds off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay.
abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.

title: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
ss_tldr: Improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training are demonstrated, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.
abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.

title: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.

title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
ss_tldr: A detector trained on per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.
abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.

title: Are We Rewarding the Wrong Module? Module-Specific Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
ss_tldr: Mod Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO) is proposed, a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules across model modules and outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.

title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning
ss_tldr: GeoSurge is presented, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces to make resection geometry learnable and editable.
abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.

title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
ss_tldr: ICLWorld is presented, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface.
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

title: A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics
ss_tldr: LOCuST is introduced, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph that describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units that a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes.
abstract: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.

title: RoboRecast: Intent-Preserving Demonstration Augmentation via Diagnosis-Driven Optimization
ss_tldr: RoboRecast is introduced, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting.
abstract: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.

title: Gated Concept Adapters: Layer-Wise Concept Bottlenecks for Auditable Text Understanding
ss_tldr: Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers, provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.
abstract: Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.

title: MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.

title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination in Language Agents
ss_tldr: Alem is introduced, a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics that makes this bottleneck measurable and provides a controlled testbed for developing agents that communicate, allocate roles, and execute shared plans.
abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, they must coordinate with others over long horizons in open-ended interactive tasks. Yet existing evaluations rarely test these demands together, focusing instead on single-agent tasks, short interactions, or highly structured multi-agent settings. We introduce $alem$, a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics. Alem embeds procedurally generated coordination tasks, soft specialisation, communication, and controllable coordination difficulty into a long-horizon survival world with exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. We evaluate $13$ LLMs zero-shot within homogeneous teams, with trained MARL agents as reference points. Current LLM agents remain far from solving alem, averaging only ~6% normalised return, but their failures are not uniform. On the hardest coordination setting, zero-shot Gemini-3.1-Pro-High approaches MARL agents trained for one billion steps, while GPT-5.4-High achieves strong base-task reward but much lower coordination reward. This contrast shows that individual task competence does not imply coordination competence. Further experiments reveal that communication is the largest contributor to coordination, while memory and reasoning help when used to maintain multi-step plans. In heterogeneous teams, however, combining different models improves base-task progress but lowers coordination reward relative to their homogeneous counterparts. Overall, our results identify coordination as a distinct bottleneck for frontier LLM agents, separate from single-agent capabilities. Alem makes this bottleneck measurable and provides a controlled testbed for developing agents that communicate, allocate roles, and execute shared plans. Code is available at https://github.com/alem-world/alem-env, with LLM traces and a leaderboard at https://alem-world.github.io.

title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
ss_tldr: The results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models, and further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting.
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

title: Emulating Non-Differentiable Metrics via Knowledge-Guided Learning: Introducing the Minkowski Image Loss
ss_tldr: This work demonstrates the necessity of coupling such topological constraints with stochastic generative architectures to achieve full morphological realism and highlights the necessity of coupling such topological constraints with stochastic generative architectures to achieve full morphological realism.
abstract: The ``differentiability gap'' presents a primary bottleneck in Earth system deep learning: since models cannot be trained directly on non-differentiable scientific metrics and must rely on smooth proxies (e.g., MSE), they often fail to capture high-frequency details, yielding ``blurry'' outputs. We develop a framework that bridges this gap using two different methods to deal with non-differentiable functions: the first is to analytically approximate the original non-differentiable function into a differentiable equivalent one; the second is to learn differentiable surrogates for scientific functionals. We formulate the analytical approximation by relaxing discrete topological operations using temperature-controlled sigmoids and continuous logical operators. Conversely, our neural emulator uses Lipschitz-convolutional neural networks to stabilize gradient learning via: (1) spectral normalization to bound the Lipschitz constant; and (2) hard architectural constraints enforcing geometric principles. We demonstrate this framework's utility by developing the Minkowski image loss, a differentiable equivalent for the integral-geometric measures of surface precipitation fields (area, perimeter, connected components). Validated on the EUMETNET OPERA dataset, our constrained neural surrogate achieves high emulation accuracy, completely eliminating the geometric violations observed in unconstrained baselines. However, applying these differentiable surrogates to a deterministic super-resolution task reveals a fundamental trade-off: while strict Lipschitz regularization ensures optimization stability, it inherently over-smooths gradient signals, restricting the recovery of highly localized convective textures. This work highlights the necessity of coupling such topological constraints with stochastic generative architectures to achieve full morphological realism.

title: From Reasoning to Code: GRPO Optimization for Underrepresented Languages
ss_tldr: A generalizable Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach that combines small-scale versions of the Qwen2.5-Coder model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to enable effective code generation through reasoning to address the limitations of sparse datasets.
abstract: Generating accurate and executable code using Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge for underrepresented programming languages, such as Prolog and Lisp, due to the scarcity of public training data compared to high-resource languages like Python. This paper introduces a generalizable Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach that combines small-scale versions of the Qwen2.5-Coder model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to enable effective code generation through reasoning. To address the limitations of sparse datasets, we integrate execution-driven feedback directly into the RL loop, utilizing a reward system that exploits both logical correctness and structural formatting. Experimental results on GSM8K dataset demonstrate significant improvements in reasoning quality and code accuracy across underrepresented languages. These findings underscore the potential of our approach to benefit a wide range of programming languages lacking extensive training resources by leveraging symbolic reasoning and interpreter-based feedback.

title: Strong Equivalence in Answer Set Programming with Constraints
ss_tldr: A translation from the language of several clingo-based answer set solvers that handle constraints into the language of Here-and-There with constraints is presented, enabling the logic of Here-and-There to reason about strong equivalence within the context of these solvers.
abstract: We investigate the concept of strong equivalence within the extended framework of Answer Set Programming with constraints. Two groups of rules are considered strongly equivalent if, informally speaking, they have the same meaning in any context. We demonstrate that, under certain assumptions, strong equivalence between rule sets in this extended setting can be precisely characterized by their equivalence in the logic of Here-and-There with constraints. Furthermore, we present a translation from the language of several clingo-based answer set solvers that handle constraints into the language of Here-and-There with constraints. This translation enables us to leverage the logic of Here-and-There to reason about strong equivalence within the context of these solvers. We also explore the computational complexity of determining strong equivalence in this context.

title: Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning
ss_tldr: Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch and avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering.
abstract: Off-dynamics offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy for a target domain using limited target data and abundant source data collected under different transition dynamics. Existing methods typically address dynamics mismatch either globally over the state space or via pointwise data filtering; these approaches can miss localized cross-domain similarities or incur high computational cost. We propose Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA), which exploits localized dynamics mismatch to better reuse source data. LoDADA clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination. Source transitions from clusters with small discrepancy are more likely to be retained compared with those from clusters with large discrepancy. This yields a fine-grained and scalable data selection strategy that avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments across environments with diverse global and local dynamics shifts. Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch.

title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire
abstract: Negative constraints (instructions of the form "do not use word X") represent a fundamental test of instruction-following capability in large language models. Despite their apparent simplicity, these constraints fail with striking regularity, and the conditions governing failure have remained poorly understood. This paper presents a mechanistic investigation of negative instruction failure in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We introduce semantic pressure, a quantitative measure of the model's intrinsic probability of generating the forbidden word, and show that violation probability rises with pressure ($p = σ(-2.95 + 2.76 P_0)$; $n=40{,}000$ samples from 2,500 prompts; prompt-bootstrap 95% CI for slope: [2.53, 3.01]), from 5% of samples at low pressure to 44% at high pressure. Comparing prompts of equal pressure, we find that the suppression induced by negative instructions is far weaker in failures: within pressure bins, the instruction lowers target probability by 0.63 less in failures than in successes (95% CI [0.61, 0.65]), and at low pressure it raises the target's probability in failures. The logit lens and direct logit attribution locate the divergence in layers 22-27, where feed-forward networks push toward the target more strongly in failures and attention pushes against it less. Activation patching shows that these late layers carry the instruction's effect in both directions. An attention-based "priming" signature does not distinguish failures from successes once its base rate is measured (90% vs. 93%); a probability-based one does (instruction raises target probability in 27% of failures vs. 13% of successes). Naming a forbidden word can prime the model to produce it, but most failures are better described as suppression that never takes hold in the final layers.

title: The Arabic AI Fingerprint: Stylometric Analysis and Detection of Large Language Models Text
ss_tldr: This work represents the most comprehensive investigation of Arabic machine-generated text to date, uniquely combining multiple prompt generation methods, diverse model architectures, and in-depth stylometric analysis across varied textual domains, establishing a foundation for developing robust, linguistically-informed detection systems essential for preserving information integrity in Arabic-language contexts.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved unprecedented capabilities in generating human-like text, posing subtle yet significant challenges for information integrity across critical domains, including education, social media, and academia, enabling sophisticated misinformation campaigns, compromising healthcare guidance, and facilitating targeted propaganda. This challenge becomes severe, particularly in under-explored and low-resource languages like Arabic. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of Arabic machine-generated text, examining multiple generation strategies (generation from the title only, content-aware generation, and text refinement) across diverse model architectures (ALLaM, Jais, Llama, and GPT-4) in academic, and social media domains. Our stylometric analysis reveals distinctive linguistic patterns differentiating human-written from machine-generated Arabic text across these varied contexts. Despite their human-like qualities, we demonstrate that LLMs produce detectable signatures in their Arabic outputs, with domain-specific characteristics that vary significantly between different contexts. Based on these insights, we developed BERT-based detection models that achieved exceptional performance in formal contexts (up to 99.9\% F1-score) with strong precision across model architectures. Our cross-domain analysis confirms generalization challenges previously reported in the literature. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the most comprehensive investigation of Arabic machine-generated text to date, uniquely combining multiple prompt generation methods, diverse model architectures, and in-depth stylometric analysis across varied textual domains, establishing a foundation for developing robust, linguistically-informed detection systems essential for preserving information integrity in Arabic-language contexts.

title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
ss_tldr: It is shown that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt, emphasizing the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction.
abstract: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
ss_tldr: This work presents a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems, and establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.
abstract: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.

title: Unpacking Interpretability: Human-Centered Criteria for Optimal Combinatorial Solutions
ss_tldr: This work studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem, in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand, and found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was.
abstract: Algorithmic support systems can return solutions that are optimal but hard to interpret for humans. A given problem can have multiple, equally optimal solutions that differ substantially in how interpretable they are. Yet there is no precise account of what makes one solution more interpretable than another. To identify structural properties associated with interpretability, we studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem (MSSP), in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand. We found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was. The strongest associations were observed for ordered representations and alignment with a greedy heuristic. Compositional simplicity also showed a consistent association. Reaction-time evidence was mixed; the only reliable result was faster responses when heuristic differences were larger. Webcam-based results of aggregate gaze times did not show reliable associations with the three solution properties. In summary, these results ground interpretability (at least in our packing paradigm) in measurable structural properties of solutions. By identifying these properties (simple compositions, ordered representation, and alignment with a heuristic) our findings motivate interpretability-aware optimization and presentation of machine solutions. They also outline a path to quantify trade-offs between optimality and interpretability in allocation and design tasks.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
ss_tldr: This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations.
abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

title: HLA: Hadamard Linear Attention
ss_tldr: Unlike previous works on linear attention, the nonlinearity in HLA is not applied separately to queries and keys, but, analogously to standard softmax attention, after the pairwise similarities have been computed.
abstract: The attention mechanism is an important reason for the success of transformers. It relies on computing pairwise relations between tokens. To reduce the high computational cost of standard quadratic attention, linear attention has been proposed as an efficient approximation. It employs kernel functions that are applied independently to the inputs before the pairwise similarities are calculated. That allows for an efficient computational procedure which, however, amounts to a low-degree rational function approximating softmax.   We propose Hadamard Linear Attention (HLA). Unlike previous works on linear attention, the nonlinearity in HLA is not applied separately to queries and keys, but, analogously to standard softmax attention, after the pairwise similarities have been computed. It will be shown that the proposed nonlinearity amounts to a higher-degree rational function to approximate softmax. An efficient computational scheme for the proposed method is derived that is similar to that of standard linear attention. In contrast to other approaches, no time-consuming tensor reshaping is necessary to apply the proposed algorithm. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated by applying it to a large diffusion transformer model for video generation, an application that involves very large amounts of tokens.

title: TopoPrune: Robust Data Pruning via Unified Latent Space Topology
ss_tldr: TopoPrune is an exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures, demonstrating a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.
abstract: Geometric data pruning methods, while practical for leveraging pretrained models, are fundamentally unstable. Their reliance on extrinsic geometry renders them highly sensitive to latent space perturbations, causing performance to degrade during cross-architecture transfer or in the presence of feature noise. We introduce TopoPrune, a framework which resolves this challenge by leveraging topology to capture the stable, intrinsic structure of data. TopoPrune operates at two scales, (1) utilizing a topology-aware manifold approximation to establish a global low-dimensional embedding of the dataset. Subsequently, (2) it employs differentiable persistent homology to perform a local topological optimization on the manifold embeddings, ranking samples by their structural complexity. We demonstrate that our unified dual-scale topological approach ensures high accuracy and precision, particularly at significant dataset pruning rates (e.g., 90%). Furthermore, through the inherent stability properties of topology, TopoPrune is (a) exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and (b) demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures. This study demonstrates a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.

title: Benchmarking LLM-Based Investment Advisor Agents for Asset Allocation in the Chinese ETF Market: Overview of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4
ss_tldr: Three core findings emerge: Native LLM reasoning capability cannot translate to superior investment returns, as models show highly differentiated risk-return characteristics; Hybrid frameworks are widely adopted, where LLMs extract textual semantic signals and quantitative modules incorporate price-volume factors and risk constraints.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) convert unstructured financial news into actionable trading strategies, yet standardized end-to-end benchmarks tailored for Chinese market remain scarce. We select common Chinese Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) as the investment universe and introduce CN-Buzz2Portfolio, the official benchmark of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4. Investment agents take daily trending Chinese financial news and historical ETF price-volume series as inputs to complete news filtering, news-to-ETF mapping and risk-controlled portfolio construction. To facilitate fair comparison, we provide a reproducible Compression--Perception--Allocation baseline compatible with mainstream LLMs. The task contains two ETF allocation tracks: Macro-Asset Allocation and Sector-Rotation Allocation. We adopt chronological data split across 2024--2026 to alleviate overfitting, with final rankings determined by out-of-sample Sharpe ratios on unseen test data. 26 teams registered for the task, and 14 submitted self-designed agent systems. Three core findings emerge: (1) Native LLM reasoning capability cannot translate to superior investment returns, as models show highly differentiated risk-return characteristics; (2) Hybrid frameworks are widely adopted, where LLMs extract textual semantic signals and quantitative modules incorporate price-volume factors and risk constraints; (3) Systems based on identical base LLMs yield distinct results with different signal processing, memory and portfolio construction modules. The project is publicly released at https://github.com/splash-li/NLPCC2026-Shared-Task-4.

title: interwhen: A Generalizable Framework for Steering Reasoning Models with Test-time Verification
ss_tldr: Interwhen is introduced, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces and achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines.
abstract: Reasoning models produce long traces of intermediate decisions and tool calls, making test-time verification important for ensuring correctness. Existing approaches either verify only the final answer, which misses early errors, or rely on branch-and-verify strategies that explore multiple trajectories. We introduce interwhen, a single-trajectory verification framework that steers model behavior by providing feedback on intermediate reasoning traces. It addresses two key challenges. First, given a set of verifiers, obtaining verifiable states from the reasoning trace typically requires prompt engineering or external task decomposition into fixed steps. Instead, we propose a monitoring system that periodically polls the reasoning trace and forks inference of the reasoning model to recover intermediate states. Verifiers are run asynchronously alongside generation, adding negligible overhead on correct executions and intervening only when violations occur. Second, beyond math and code, a central challenge for process verification is the scarcity of verifiers. interwhen addresses this through automatic verifier synthesis from natural-language policy documents. Given a policy, it can generate code-based verifiers, including provably correct verifiers in Lean and z3. Together, these contributions yield a plug-and-play test-time verification system that can improve task completion and policy compliance of any reasoning agent. On reasoning benchmarks where policies encode mathematical or logical constraints, interwhen achieves near-perfect accuracy for reasoning models using a fraction of the tokens of baselines. On agentic benchmarks with policy-based verifier generation, it enables improvements in task quality for SLMs without any finetuning, e.g., task completion rate of Qwen3-30B jumps from 32% to 87% on the telecom domain in tau2-bench. Code at https://github.com/microsoft/interwhen.

title: ReviewSense: Cluster-Guided Evidence Selection for Actionable Review-to-Advice Generation
ss_tldr: Evaluating on dental and healthcare service reviews with expert judgment of actionability and annotator-based theme alignment, it is found that a single central representative preserves the dominant cluster theme in 77.3% of cases but only 60.6% of secondary themes: central evidence captures main issues more reliably than minority concerns.
abstract: Customer reviews are a rich but weakly structured source of operational feedback. We study ReviewSense, a cluster-guided evidence-selection workflow that converts review corpora into action-oriented advice for human decision support. Reviews are embedded with a sentence transformer, grouped by iterative cosine-similarity clustering with threshold decay, and reduced to compact evidence before Large Language Model (LLM) generation. Evaluating on dental and healthcare service reviews with expert judgment of actionability and annotator-based theme alignment, we find that a single central representative preserves the dominant cluster theme in 77.3% of cases but only 60.6% of secondary themes: central evidence captures main issues more reliably than minority concerns. Against fixed-generator LLM baselines, five cluster representatives yield the advice closest to expert recommendations while using a fraction of the raw-review context, whereas a single representative is not the strongest front-end. Across three domains the clustering assigns every review while remaining competitive with standard algorithms. Our contribution is therefore an empirical account of evidence selection as the controlling design variable in review-to-advice generation, delivered as an inspectable human-in-the-loop workflow rather than a new clustering algorithm or a general review summarizer.

title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
ss_tldr: RMU is developed, a state-of-the-art unlearning method based on controlling model representations that reduces model performance on WMDP while maintaining general capabilities in areas such as biology and computer science, suggesting that unlearning may be a concrete path towards reducing malicious use from LLMs.
abstract: The White House AI Action Plan highlights the risks of large language models (LLMs) empowering malicious actors in developing biological, cyber, and chemical weapons. To measure these risks, government institutions and major AI labs are developing evaluations for hazardous capabilities in LLMs. However, current evaluations are private, preventing further research into mitigating risk. Furthermore, they focus on only a few, highly specific pathways for malicious use. To fill these gaps, we publicly release the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) benchmark, a dataset of 3,668 multiple-choice questions that serve as a proxy measurement of hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity, and chemical security. WMDP was developed by a consortium of academics and technical consultants, and was stringently filtered to eliminate sensitive information prior to public release. WMDP serves two roles: first, as an evaluation for hazardous knowledge in LLMs, and second, as a benchmark for unlearning methods to remove such hazardous knowledge. To guide progress on unlearning, we develop RMU, a state-of-the-art unlearning method based on controlling model representations. RMU reduces model performance on WMDP while maintaining general capabilities in areas such as biology and computer science, suggesting that unlearning may be a concrete path towards reducing malicious use from LLMs. We release our benchmark and code publicly at https://wmdp.ai

title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
ss_tldr: The proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
abstract: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.

title: A Threshold Model of Fault Propagation in AI-Native Software Ecosystems
ss_tldr: This paper model how a fault spreads among open changes as a branching process over contention, the relation between two changes that are open at the same time and modify a common file, and reconstructs contention among 33,105 agent-authored pull requests.
abstract: When many coding agents work in one repository at once, software engineers are left to judge a collective through its parts. Review examines one change at a time, yet a change can incorporate a fault introduced by another, and repairing the originating change then no longer repairs the repository. To keep human judgment at the centre of agentic software development, we need models of what agents do together. This paper joins complexity theory with software evolution to build one. We model how a fault spreads among open changes as a branching process over contention, the relation between two changes that are open at the same time and modify a common file. As with the reproduction number of an epidemic, spread sustains itself once each faulty change passes the fault, on average, to more than one other. Each repository has a reference threshold, the crossing probability per contention link above which spread would sustain itself in a random graph with the repository's contention degrees. We reconstructed contention among 33,105 agent-authored pull requests in 2,731 repositories. Thirteen repositories with reference thresholds below 5% contained 42.5% of the changes. There, a fault that crossed one contention link in twenty would sustain spread under the model. The structural conditions for propagation are in place where much agent-authored work happens. Reviewing each change separately cannot reveal these conditions. Engineers also need to know where concurrent work exposes a repository to spreading faults, which they can compute from records they already keep.

title: MathConstruct: Challenging LLM Reasoning with Constructive Proofs
ss_tldr: This work introduces MathConstruct, a new benchmark of 121 challenging problems sourced from various math competitions, which targets constructive proofs, a widely encountered problem type requiring the construction of mathematical objects with specific properties.
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance in mathematics, existing math benchmarks come with significant limitations. Many focus on problems with fixed ground-truth answers, and are often saturated due to problem simplicity or the viability of guessing or memorization. Crucially, they capture only a narrow subset of relevant math problems. To address this research gap, we introduce MathConstruct, a new benchmark of 121 challenging problems sourced from various math competitions, which targets constructive proofs, a widely encountered problem type requiring the construction of mathematical objects with specific properties. These proofs are particularly suitable for LLM evaluation, as solution correctness can be easily verified. Our automated verifiers also enable MathConstruct to generate problem variations, used to evaluate robustness. State-of-the-art LLMs solve only 60% of MathConstruct problems, highlighting its complexity and importance for LLM evaluation.

title: Polyrating: A Cost-Effective and Bias-Aware Rating System for LLM Evaluation
ss_tldr: Polyrating is introduced, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs and can reduce the cost of human evaluations.
abstract: Rating-based human evaluation has become an essential tool to accurately evaluate the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs). However, current rating systems suffer from several important limitations: first, they fail to account for biases that significantly influence evaluation results, second, they require large and expensive preference datasets to obtain accurate ratings, and third, they do not facilitate meaningful comparisons of model ratings across different tasks. To address these issues, we introduce Polyrating, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs. Polyrating can detect and quantify biases affecting human preferences, ensuring fairer model comparisons. Further, Polyrating can reduce the cost of human evaluations by up to $59\%$ for new models and up to $77\%$ for new tasks by leveraging existing benchmark scores. Lastly, Polyrating enables direct comparisons of ratings across different tasks, providing a comprehensive understanding of an LLMs' strengths, weaknesses, and relative performance across different applications.

title: Predictive Coding Implemented as a Hardware Substrate Computes Gradients faster than Backpropagation
ss_tldr: This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron.
abstract: Backpropagation has enabled modern deep learning but is difficult to realize as an online, fully distributed hardware system due to global error propagation, separate phases, and centralized memory. Predictive coding is an alternative learning algorithm with similar dynamics to backpropagation that arises from local prediction error dynamics. This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron. Each core stores its own activity and weights, communicates with the cores that it's connected to, and performs local gradient updates. By updating neuron cores concurrently, the architecture computes a network update in O(J+K) clock cycles.
